222    Government  [RAJYA SABHA]  Resolution  

DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI (Rajasthan): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I rise at this 
late hour to speak on a subject on which several Me mbers have spoken earlier, but the 
subject itself is so interesting, "Karnataka mein n atak", that I am sure I should be able to 
hold your attention for about five or ten mintues. Sir, this is a play which has all the essential 
ingredients of a successful drama. It has tragedy, it has comedy, it has pathos, it has a huge 
amount of free entertainment.. (Interruptions)...  
SHRI AMAR SINGH (Uttar Pradesh): What is your role? 
DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: It has a villain. The on ly problem is it has no 
heroes ... (Interruptions)...  
SHRI AMAR SINGH: What is your role in it? 
DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: I will tell you about our role. Our role is to scrupulously 
follow the text-book, but I will come to our role a  little later. This is, Sir, a theatre of the 
absurd. This is a sordid saga and each of these words is not a mere adjective, but they have 
meaning. They have been made pregnant with meaning by the two principal dramatist 
personnel of that State. This is a sordid saga of c orruption, mismanagement, opportunism, 
hypocrisy, unholy alliances, and, of course, above all, loot of the State. Sir, in a sense, it is 
a great victory for democracy; it is also a failure of democracy. It is a victory of democracy 
because we have, at least, now very shortly a corre ctive and, hopefully, we will go to the 
polls. But it is a failure in the sense that so long this kind of a farce could go on in the form 
of Government. It illustrates a naked lust for power. There is a Party, the Party whose former 
President spoke some time ago, whose righteous indi gnation is completely misplaced. 
There is a Party which saw the writing on the wall. 
They knew the facts. They turned a Nelsonian blind eye to reality only because of their 
lust for power. They became an ostrich in the sand because they could not stay without 
power and their greed for power drove them into the so-called alliance. 
My friend, Mr. Amar Singh, asked about our role. Well, let us tell him about our role. Our 
role is to point out from day one the inherently unstable nature of the proposed alliance, of 
the Government-formation process. We said, 'it cann ot last; there is internal contradiction; 
it will not last.' And, we, therefore, as the Congr ess, said that the Government would be 
within its right to dissolve it and to go to the pe ople. And, what did the Congress-led UPA 
Government do? The Congress-led UPA Government foll owed a textbook example of 
scrupulous morality to a fault. The scrupulous morality to a fault was that although there is 
a view that in law even under Bommai, it could have been dissolved then. It did not do so  
despite the obvious elements of inherent instability, and, therefore, we bent over backwards 
to give some time, if possible, even remotely possi ble, thereby, giving you, perhaps, the 
shortest-lived Government in South India, if that i s of some satisfaction to the main 
Opposition of this House. 
SHRI AMAR SINGH: What about Dave Gowda and Dharam Singh Alliance? 
DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: Mr. Amar Singh will not dictate the sequence of my 
speech. Permit me to speak in my own way. I will deal with them as well. You are the only one, 
perhaps, we will not deal with this time, but we will deal with all the other parties. 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, this is the theatre of the absurd for another reason. It is for the 
first time, probably, in constitutional history, in democratic history, that you have the concept 

Government  [26 NOV. 2007]  Resolution   223 
of collective responsibility turned over on its hea d. It is not only collective 
irresponsibility. It is collective irresponsibility  with murder charges being traded in the 
Cabinet between none else than a Cabinet Minister a nd the Chief Minister. It is a case 
unprecedented in global parliamentary history of a sitting Minister trading corruption 
charges. It is a case unprecedented globally, not i n India, not in Karnataka alone, of full-
page advertisements by the two principal partners w ho are supposed to be in alliance in 
running a State, full-page advertisements, carrying  out a campaign one against the other. 
Well, this is collective responsibility as per the definition of the BJP or the JD(S)! Mr. 
Deputy Chairman, Sir, this naked lust for power, this ostrich-in-sand attitude, led the BJP to 
arrive in full form, full force with a Bharat for the remarriage. Unfortunately, for them, it is 
before the 'punervivah', there was a t alak'. There was a divorce. All the beautiful dreams of 
honeymoon were shattered (Interruptions) Yes; Mr. Ahluwalia, you made a small mistake. 
You arrived with the barat, but you made a small omission. You forgot to take the consent 
of the bride. That is why, the dreams of the honeymoon were shattered before it began. 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, my time is short. In the formulation 'JD(S)', all of us know now 
that the word 'S', is the biggest joke on the polit ical firmament of this system. To say that 
they still practise secularism or believe in secularism, after all the shenanigans and all the 
acrobatics in the last few years, is truly a sad and tragic joke on this nation. 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, Article 356, of course, was made by our Constitution-framers 
to provide for a failure of constitutional machinery. But failure of constitutional machinery, 
I beg to submit, Sir, also includes gross extreme forms of misgovernance. There was nothing 
short of loot of the State going on and Article 356 has not come or rather dissolution has not 
come a day too early. I had this very strange example in this State which is again unheard 
of The State is divided up as if by a legal contract. Since when have you heard that a State 
is divided up by a MoU? Our Indian Contract Act has  so many provisions but the British 
never dreamt of it, the Indians never dreamt of it,  to have a clause that the State's loot can 
be divided by a twelve-condition MoU, and if you do n't sign the MoU, you must then go 
and break the Government or you must decide how to share the spoils of war. Each of the 
events, Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, is unprecedented in parliamentary democracy; it is unheard 
of anywhere and only one word is suitable for these  two parties, 'shame on them', 'shame 
on their so-called principles', 'shame on their conduct,' 'shame on what they did in Karnataka

STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS—Contd.  
Violence by all adivashi students association of Assam on 24th November, 2007 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAI RS (SHRI 
SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): Hon'ble Deputy Chairman, Sir, I rise, with a deep sense of 
anguish, to inform this august House of the violenc e which took place in Guwahati on 
24th Nov., 2007. The Government of Assam has informed that:— 
All Adivashi Students Association of Assam (AASAA) had applied to District Magistrate, 
Guwahati on 6.11.07 for holding a Gana Samabesh (rally) on 24.11.07 at Guwahati in the 
South Beltola School field to press for their demand of declaring the Adivashis in Assam as 
Scheduled Tribes (Plains). No permission was grante d to the Association for holding the 
rally. However, the people brought by AASAA started  gathering in the field of South 
Beltola High School from the morning of 24.11.07. About 3000 to 3500 people gathered at the 
site by 11.30 AM. Most of the people came from the districts of Kokrajhar, Karbi Anglong, 
Darrang, Udalguri, Golaghat etc., in about 50-60 buses. After gathering they wanted to take 
out a procession to the Dispur Capital complex. 
They were not given permission by the Magistrate on  duty to take out the procession. 
But, about 1000-1500 persons broke away forcefully by overpowering the Police pickets at 
aroung 12.00 noon and entered the Bassistha Road leading to Dispur Capital complex from 
Beltola. On the way they reportedly indulged in van dalism and damage to shops and cars 
by pelting stones and using the lathis, bows and ar rows, which they were carrying with 
them. 
More than 50 vehicles and 30 shops are said to have  been damaged in the process. 
When the processionists reached near the entrance t o the MLA's Hostel, the Police party 
dispersed them by mild lathi charge and fired tear gas shells. On being disperse d, the 
processionists ran in different directions and ente red different byelanes in the area in 
addition to the main Basistha road. While they were dispersing the persons affected by the 
violence, these people retaliated and attacked them . As a result, number of processionists 
and agitationists were injured. The situation was b rought under control by 1.00 p.m. on 
24th Nov., 2007, with the arrival of additional police force. 
All the injured persons were shifted to Guwahati Medical College Hospital and Mahendra 
Mohan Choudhury Civil Hospital. The total number of persons injured is 242, out of which, 
10 persons have been injured seriously. One person succumbed to his injury in the Hospital 
in the evening. The identity of the dead person is yet to be ascertained. Fifty-seven persons 
have been discharged and sent back to their respect ive districts on 25.11.07. All steps are 
beign taken to give free medical treatment. It is expected that all the remaining persons other 
than the ten seriously injured persons will be discharged and sent to their respective home 
districts by 26.11.07 forenoon. 
The District Magistrate imposed curfew, as a precautionary measure, from 2.25 p.m. on 
24.11.07, which had been relaxed for 12 hours from 8.00 a.m. on 25.11.07. The curfew has 
been withdrawn from 8.00 p.m. on 25th November, 2007. On 24th November, 2007, after the 
incident, about 2000 persons, who were in the meeti ng ground, were safely sent back to 
their districts with police escort in the evening in the vehicles brought by them. About 900 
people were rescued from different roads and byelanes and they were taken to Basistha 

Statement  [26 NOV. 2007]  by Ministers   227 
Thana and sent to their respective home districts by 25th November morning under police 
escort. 
The State Government has already announced ex-gratia of Rs. 3 lakhs to the next of kin 
of the person killed and Rs. 50,000/- to the persons seriously injured and Rs. 10,000/- to the 
persons with simple injury. An enquiry by Shri P.P. Verma, Additional Chief Secretary, has 
been ordered. 
The situation at present is peaceful and under watch. The AASAA has given a call for 36 
hours Assam bandh from 5.00 a.m. of 26.11.07 to 5.00 p.m. of 27.11.07. 
A close watch is being kept on the situation. The senior officers of the Ministry of Home 
Affairs are in constant touch with the Chief Secretary and DGP of the State.

SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, we have no objection. 
SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL: Sir, there has been a dem and for giving Scheduled 
Tribe (ST) status to Tea and ex-tea garden communit ies comprising Munda, Oran, Gonds, 
Santhals etc., from Bihar, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh e tc. This has been examined several 
times by the office of RGI. The Lokur Committee had also considered this issue in 1965, and 
had noted that they agreed with the opinion of the Backward Classes Commission and did 
not recommend the tea plantation .labourers to be t reated as STs. The settlers in the tea 
estates have tended to lose their tribal characteri stics in the new surroundings. Moreover, 
the office of RGI noted that many of the tea tribe communities were not STs even in their 
native States i.e. Basor, Bhattar, Basphoor, Bhagta, Tandoi, etc. were SC in the native states 
while Bhamij, Beha, etc. were listed as SC/ST in di fferent States of origin. Based on these 
considerations and the observations of the Lokur Co mmittee, as well as the Backward 
Classes Commission, RGI has not supported the proposal of the State Govt. for inclusion of 
tea tribes in the list of STs in Assam. The Government of Assam had also initially consistently 
opposed giving them the ST status. 
A close watch is being kept on the situation. The senior officers of the Ministry of 
Home Affairs are in constant touch with the Chief Secretary and DGP of the State.

SHRI SHIVRAJ V PATIL: The point I was making was that there are some constraints 
under which Governments have to function. We have the Constitution. We follow the rule 
of law. There are laws which have to be followed by us. If we do not follow those laws, we 
will not be able to function. Now, having functione d in the last sixty years, if somethings 
have come to our notice, let us consider them in the House and outside and let us try to find 
a solution to them. 
Sir, I am ve:y pained to say that so many Policemen  are dying while protecting the life 
and property of our people. A Policeman coming from Kerala dies in Assam while protecting 
his brother's life and property in Assam. We do not care for him. But, then, he becomes the 
target. And the man who actually fires the bullet, the man who actually explodes the bombs, 
is forgotten. The second target is the Government, whether it belongs to this party or that 
party. We are not tackling the issue as such. I am saying that the injury is at one place and 
you are applying the medicine at some other place and that is why it has not been possible 
for us to contain violence. It is very easy for me to complain against the UP Government, to 
complain against the West bengal Government, to com plain against the Chhattisgarh 
Government and say, "Well, this should have been do ne by you. This is the constitution". 
But I am not doing it. I am not doing it in the House and I am not doing it outside also. But 
we have persons who are not interested in having so mething which is balanced, which is

not answer the real question that is posed in the H ouse. The real question that is posed in 
the House is this. Terrorism is growing; bomb blasts are taking place and there is terrorism

activities are on the rise. The House would like to  know about the political strategy of the

with differenet names. We have seen Tamil Tigers' terrorism, Sikh terrorism, Naxalite terrorism, 
Jammu & Kashmir terrorism why only talk of muslim terrorism. We have seen terrorism of 
different kinds.

Reduction in Government Equity in Public Sector Banks  
   †* 161. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI :†† 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Chairman, Economic Ad visory Council to Prime 
Minister has advised to reduce Government equity in  Public Sector Banks in the 
country to less than 51 percent; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard and the reaction of Government in respect of this 
advice; and 
(c) the share of Indian and Foreign investors' equity in each Public Sector Bank till 
the end of September, 2007? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha. 
(a) and (b) No, Sir. However, in his inaugural addr ess at a Conference on Global 
Banking, entitled "Theme: Managing Transition" organized by Federation of Indian 
Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Chairman, Economic Advisory Council to the 
Prime Minister has made certain observations in the context of capital adequacy of the 
public sector banks. To ensure rapid growth of publ ic sector banks (PSBs), he 
suggested that the Government may have to either br ing in additional capital in 
these banks, or reduce its share below 51% through appropriate statutory changes, or 
include in the definition of the 'Government' such entities which are quasi-Government 
in nature and are likely to remain to be fully owne d or an integral part of the 
Government system in the future. 
There is no proposal under consideration to amend t he statutory or other 
provisions for enabling the Government to bring dow n its shareholding in the 
PSBs, (other than Associate Banks of State Bank of India (SBI) where Government 
has no shareholding) to below 51%. 
(c) The share of resident and non-resident holdings in the quity capital of PSBs, as 
at the end of September, 2007, is given in the enclosed Statement-I.

DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, I am happy that the h on. Minister has 
made a statement that there is no proposal to reduc e the equity of the public sector 
banks. But, what is the actual policy and intention of this Government? Will the hon. 
Minister assure the House that this Government will  not reduce the Government's 
share in the PSBs and will not allow it to come dow n less than 51 per cent as it is 
today? And, what steps the Government intends to ta ke so that adequate capital is 
available to the PSBs so that they can compete and grow not only in India but also 
compete with foreign banks and grow abroad? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, my good friend is smiling  at me. So, I think, he 
is in a good today. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Whenever I see your face, I am always in a 
good mood. But, it is only after your statements. I get into a bad mood. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: I think he takes it in good sp irit. Coming to the 
question, Sir, it is the previous Government which had proposed that the equity 
should be reduced to 33 per cent. But, since this G overnment assumed office, I 
made it clear that the equity of the 

Oral Answers [27 NOV. 2007]                   to Questions     5  
Government in the public sector banks will not be reduced below 51 per cent. That 
statement stands. So, we have no proposal to reduce it to below 51 per cent. 
Now, as far as providing more capital is concerned,  guidelines have been issued 
by the Reserve Bank of India on what would be regar ded as Tier-I capital. We have 
to meet the Basel-II Norms. The RBI's guidelines on Tier-I capital are being followed 
by banks. We have various options to raise the Tier -I capital, depending upon the 
factual situation with regard to each bank; we can use one alternative or the other. But, 
our policy is, we will ensure that all our banks ha ve adequate capital strictly in 
accordance with the Basel-II Norms. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI. Sir, the second supplement ary is: If you allow 
more funds to come to the banks, it will be contrib uting towards inflation also. The 
appreciation of rupee has also a consequence on the capital market. So, may I ask the 
hon. Minister to inform the House about the steps b eing taken for making adequate 
micro economic management policies? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, there is another question  which I have 
answered on the steps being taken to manage the mon etary situation. But, briefly, 
there is, of course, a large flow—export earnings, remittances from workers, FDI, 
foreign institutional investment, private equity, etc.—of capital into India. All this, of 
course, is good if we can absorb the inflows and tu rn it into productive investment. 
But, since this question relates to banking, any capital that flows into bank enhances 
the bank's capital base. This, of course, is regula ted by the RBI. It is not as though 
any one can buy the equity of any bank. There are v ery strict regulations. The FH's 
is capped at 20 per cent, no individual shareholder  can buy more than 5 per cent 
without regulatory approval. Sir, the Government will never sell its equity so that it 
comes below 51 per cent. Therefore, there is no rus h of capital into our banking 
system. Of course, there are foreign banks, to the extent they are permitted, they can 
bring in capital for their own operation. But the inflows into India are into different 
sectors. There is no uncontrolled inflow into the b anking sector because the flow of 
capital to the banking sector is very strictly regulated by the RBI's guidelines. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: It is true that banks are guided by the RBI's 
guidelines. But when there is an inflow of capital and if it raises inflation, then, you 
control the banks' outflow for investments. My supp lementary is this. This is a very 
complicated question of macro economic management. Will you inform us that the 
movement of rupee, inflows and adequate capital to banks will be adequately 
handled in terms of macro economic management? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: That is true. There are large inflows into other 
sectors, and if it is giving rise to inflationary e xpectations or giving rise to inflation, 
the RBI will have to make changes in the monetary p olicy, and changes in the 
monetary policy will indeed be reflected in the interest rates of banks. I entirely agree 
with what the hon. Member says. All I am pointing o ut is that this question concerns 
the capital in banks. My answer is, flow of capital into banks is strictly regulated, and 
the large inflows that we see, into some other sect ors, does not really affect the 
banking sector. Of course, when we come to the other supplementary, there is separate 
question which I will answer then. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: You can answer it right now. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: I do not know if the Chairman will permit me to 
answer beyond the scope of the question. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri Raj Mohinder Singh Majitha. Not present. Shri D. Raja.

(d) The Approach Paper to the Eleventh Plan has endorsed a vision of delivering faster 
and more inclusive growth. To this end, it has set a target of 9 percent per annum GDP 
growth for the country as a whole to be achieved in a manner that would ensure greater 
inclusiveness of the growth process. The Approach Paper has also set monitorable targets in 
the areas of income and poverty, education, health,  women and children issues, 
infrastructure and environment, reflecting the inclusiveness of this growth. The Approach 
Paper also mentions about reducing the disparities across regions by ensuring access to 
basic physical infrastructure as well as health and education services to all. The copies of 
the Approach Paper have been placed in the Parliament library. 
The Central Government has adopted a multi pronged strategy to reduce the divide 
between urban and rural India Bharat Nirman, a time bound business plan for addressing the 
gap in rural infrastructure covering irrigation, ro ad connectivity, water supply, rural 
electrification, housing and rural telecom connectivity. The Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana implemented by Panchayati Raj Institutions seeks to create durable community 
assets in rural areas. The National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme attempts to 
ensure a social safety net as it provides guaranteed employment in rural areas. It can also 
become instrumental in building rural infrastructure. The National Rural Health Mission 
and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan are programmes for delivering primary health services and 
elementary education respectively. 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY; Sir, Sengupta Committee Re port has been 
submitted to the Prime Minister. According to that Report, 21.8 per cent of the people are 
living below the poverty line. They are the poorest of the poort. Their income, according to 
the Sengupta Report below Rs. 20. Now the hon. Mini ster for Planning, Shri M. V. 
Rajasekharan, who is sitting here beside me, in his reply to Unstarred Question No. 534 
mentioned the consumption expenditure of people below and above the poverty line in 
2004-05. He stated, in his reply, that the rural BPL income per month was Rs. 286.13, 
that is, about Rs. 9.50 per day and the rural APL income was Rs. 660.67 per month, that 
is, about Rs. 20 per day. Now, the question before the nation is whether the Government 
has taken cognizance of this fact, particularly the report of the Sengupta Committee which 
had been constituted by you. I am saying this because you are for the poor people and 
your heart is bleeding for the poor people. But here is a case wherein they get just Rs. 
9.50 per day for their consumption. How can they li ve? Only saying that we are 
monitoring it and we are giving something to them, will not be sufficient. 
MR. CHAIRMAN:  Question please. 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: What concrete steps have b een taken by the 
government after the submission of this Report? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the consumption estimates have been made for rural 
and urban India by the National Sample Survey Organisation and the Sengupta Report also 
draws heavily on the NSSO Survey. According to this Survey, the monthly per capita 
consumption expenditure at current prices in 2004-05 for rural India was Rs. 558 and for 
urban India, it was Rs. 1052. Obviously, at this level of consumption, it is reasonable 
conclusion that a large number of people are poor. In fact, the poverty estimates made 
indicate that the poverty proportion in 2004-05 was 28 per cent. The Planning commission 
estimates that this proportion would have come down in the last three years. 
Now, the anser to this is to follow theeconomic pol icies that promote a more 
inclusive growth. Growth is an imperative. Inclusive growth is what we should aim at. 
It is for that purpose that we have announced a number of flagship programmes and we have 
also announced 

8        Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA]                             to Questions  
a very large and ambitious programme for rural Indi a under the name of Bharat 
Nirman. The National rural Employment Guarantee Pro gramme, the National rural 
Health Mission, thevast expansion of the ICDS, the Debt and Disability Insurance 
under the Aam Adami Bima Yojana introduced .recentl y, and the Rashtriya 
Swasthaya Bima Yojana that has been offered to the State Governments, are 
programme which will fill critical gaps which contr ibute to poverty. Besides, there 
are clear targets set for Bharat Nirman—every villa ge to have electricity, every 
habitation to have all—weather road, every habitati on to have safe drinking water, 
every village to be connected by telephone and to b uild 60 lakh houses for the rural 
poor. The completion of Bharat Nirman will also bring a large number of services to 
the poor. So, while these measures will address non -income aspects of poverty, the 
way to address poverty is to raise the incomes of t hose who are poor today. Since 
many of them are engaged in agriculture, the goal is to raise the agricultural growth 
to, at least, four per cent a year so that they hav e a larger agricultural income. I think, 
a multi-pronged attack looking at increasing income s, filling critical gaps and 
addressing non-income aspect of poverty, altogether, will bring down poverty in the 
medium-term. 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Sir, the Deputy Chairman, Planning 
Commission, has stated that about 58 per cent of th e subsidized foodgrains issued 
from the Central pool do not reach the weaker secti ons. Further, he has stated out of 
one rupee from the Budgetary allocations of subsidy  to poorer sections, what is the 
amount that is reaching them; only 27 paisa is reaching. 
Sir, if you kindly take into consideration the income of 36 big industrialists in the 
country, that comes to Rs. 8,66,000 crores. That is  reported in the newspapers. The 
Central revenue receipts is to the tune of Rs. 4,33 ,231 crores. The entire income of 
the national is in the hands of a few people. We ha ve to give a thrust to the rural 
people and particularly, for the poorer people. Sma ll-scale industries are there, 
there is agricultural sector. So far as the banking  sector is concerned, we are giving 
only 40 per cent of the disbursal to this sector as  a priority sector. I would like to 
know whether the Government, in order give financia l strength to the agricultural 
sector and the small-scale sector as also the landl ess labourers, proposes to increase 
the percentage of disbursal from 40 to 50. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, as I said, there are a large number of claims from 
different sectors upon Budgetary resources as well as resources from the banking 
system. No policy is cast in stone. All these polic ies are adjusted and fine-turned 
based upon experience. Today, the policy is that 40  per cent of all bank lending 
should go to the priority sector. Within the priority sector, we have, I believe and I say 
this most humbly, increased the lending to agricultural sector from Rs. 86,000 crores in 
2003-04 to Rs. 2,25,000 crores, perhaps more, in th e current year. Likewise, to the 
small and medium enterprises, we have said we will double it in five years, increase 
it by 20 per cent every year. We have increased it by over 20 per cent in the first year; 
the current year is the second year. We will increa se it by over 20 per cent in the 
second year too. 
I acknowledge the thrust and passion behind the que stion of the hon. Member. 
For each sector, policies have been devised. Polici es are implemented by respective 
Ministries or Departments working with the State Go vernments. It is possible that 
some policies are working well in some places and not working well in other places. He 
did mention the Public Distribution System. It is a sad fact that a significant portion of 
grain, I do not have the numbers off-hand, in the Public distribution System is indeed

delivered is again a function of governance. Good g overnance means that the grains 
are delivered through the Public Distribution System. While the governance is a major 
problem in delivery of goods and services to the poor, I think, policies are fine-tuned 
from time to time. If hon. Members have suggestions , to modify current policies, I 
am sure, everyone in the government is open to thos e suggestions and we will fine-
tune the policies as we go along.

proposes a very large increase for fertilizer subsidy because fertilizer prices have gone 
up, the prices of raw materials have gone up. There fore, we are in the Second 
Supplementary, which will come before this House da y after tomorrow, there is a 
very sharp rise in the fertilizer subsidy. Sir, as far as changing policies is 
concerned, yes, there is, of course, a sharp differ ence of opinion about what 
economic policy should be followed. I respect the policies of each party. But as far as 
the UPA Government is concerned, our policies are s pelt out in the NOMP. We are 
indeed following a policy based on economic reforms  initiated in 1991 and over 
the last 15 years,

these policies have been fine-tuned to ensure that there is growth as well as more 
inclusive growth. In fact, when the new Plan docume nt, will come up before the

growth.

are also conscious that faster growth is not enough . It must be more inclusive. That 
is why a whole range of programmes from NREGP to ex panding ICDS, to which I

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, as far income poverty is concerned, the answer is to 
raise peoples' income. The agricultural sector is growing at about 3.2 to 3.3 per cent in the 
last three years. The goal is to raise it to four per cent. 
MS. MABEL REBELLO: Sir, that is in some areas where there is irrigation. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please do not interrupt. 
MS. MABEL REBELLO: In tribal areas, where there is no irrigation, the people's

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, may I complete the reply to her? I was replying and 
she then wanted to say something and so I sat down. As far as the agriculture income 
poverty is concerned, if large proportions of rural people are engaged in agriculture and 
their income is solely dependent on agriculture, unless the agriculture sector grows at a 
reasonable rate of four per cent, their incomes will not rise. That is why the policies have 
been devised. The Minister of Agriculture has placed the policy how to raise growth 
rate of the agriculture sector to 4 per cent. Therefore, if the agriculture income rises the 
income poverty of the sector that is dependant on agriculture will be mitigated. But, as I 
said, poverty is not only income poverty, poverty i s measured by other non-income 
parameters and that we are addressing through the Bharat Nirman, through the NREGS, 
through the NRHM, SSA, through the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, through the ICDS, etc. 
These are the programmes intended to target the non-income aspects of poverty. If these 
programmes are delivered properly, when the services are delivered effectively by good 
governance, it will make a difference to the poverty status of the poor.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: You have asked your question, you must listen to

Therefore, Sir, some migration is unavoidable. In f act, in every country, there 
has been migration from rural parts of the country to the urban parts. The point is, if 
land holding is small as it is and land holding get s fragmented, a number of people 
cannot earn an adequate income from the land and th ey will migrate to places where 
they can find jobs. Today, the agriculture sector r epresents about 18 per cent of the 
GDP and about 60 per cent of the working population  is dependent on agriculture. 
That is why incomes are low. But in the other two sectors which are growing at a faster 
rate, and a smaller proportion of population is dependent on them, the income is high. 
Therefore, between the people who are engaged in ag riculture on the one hand and 
people who are engaged in services and industry on the other, there is, indeed, a 
widening disparity in income. That is why the answe r is to try to raise agriculture 
income. At the risk of repetition, let me say, we must ensure that the agriculture sector 
grows at 4 per cent and, as a result, income from a griculture also rises. In the 
meanwhile, if the industry and services do well, people who are depending on industry 
and services, people who earn their livelihood thro ugh industry and services will 
indeed, get higher incomes and we cannot grudge those higher incomes. They are not 
rich people. Some rich people are there. But most o f the working people in industry 
and services are people who are entitled to higher incomes. Sir, that is the reason for 
this divide. We are addressing it by accelerating g rowth. But that is not enough. We 
need to fill in the critical gaps in literacy, in e ducation, in health care, in roads and 
electric connectivity, and in other services. I have narrated all the programmes, which 
have been launched by this Government, and which th is Government has continued 
from the previous Governments, are intended to meet these critical gaps in rural India. 
For example, one such programme is the RIDF. We sta rted the RIDF with a modest 
outlay of about Rs. 1,000 crores, I think, in the y ear 1994-95. Today, the RIDF has 
an outlay of Rs. 12,000 crores, with an additional window of Rs. 4,000 crores for rural 
roads. So, the funds to the tune of Rs. 16,000 from  in the banking system are being 
given to the States for rural infrastructure. Where the money is well spent; where there 
is good governance; where the roads are laid; where  the water supply is made 
available, it does bring benefit to the poor. But w here the governance has collapsed; 
where there is poor governance; where there is no delivery, merely spending money is 
not going to help. The challenge, therefore, is not  only to find the money, which we 
do, the challenge is to spend the money efficiently , which is the function of 
governance. And, I am sorry to say, in many parts o f India, governance is in a poor 
state. (Interruptions)

National Culture Policy  
*164.    SHRIMATI SHOBHANA  BHARTIA††  
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Committee was constituted by her Ministry  in October last year 
with the responsibility of making recommendations t o the Ministry for framing a 
National Culture Policy and was asked to study, amo ng other things, the extent and 
role of Government in various areas of culture and also assess the mandate for 
various cultural institutions;

(c) whether Government has received the report; and 
(d) if so, the details of the same?

months of its constitutions.

necessary for the Government to have a fixed policy  in the matters of art and

declare that I have an interest, in the sense, that  I also happen to be the President of 
the Indian Council for Cultural Relations. 
Sir, it is shocking that the Committee, set up over  a year ago, has met only once, 
and, then, out of 19 members only 8 members attende d it. What sort of a farce is 
this? What sort of committees do we appoint if they  are not prepared to come to 
meetings? That is the first thing I want to say. Th is is the first observation. This 
shows that there is no sense of urgency about this matter. 
But, Sir, the real point I want to make is this. Shri Chidambaram is trying to make 
us into an economic superpower. We all want to beco me political superpowers. We 
are a cultural superpower. There is no doubt about it. We are one of the few nations 
in the world that can claim to be a cultural superp ower. Our culture, without the use 
of arms, has spread down through the centuries, dow n through the corridors of time 
throughout vast swathes of South and South East Asi a. Now, therefore, we must 
give culture top priority. If this is the sort of a ttitude that is going to be taken by the 
members of the committee, I am afraid, Sir, it is n ot a good omen. May I therefore 
know from the hon. Minister whether he will, first of all, have wide-ranging 
consultations? There are organisations, like the IC CR, and there are private cultural 
organisations. There are literary organisations. Cu lture involves dance, music, art, 
architecture, philosophy, language; there is the wh ole gamut of what makes a 
human being

civilised. Will they spread their net wider? Will they try and get the best minds in 
India involved, before they come out with a cultural policy? 
SHRI AJAY MAKEN: Sir, in the Committee to formulate  the cultural policy as 
well as the Central Advisory Board on Culture, the Ministry always tries to have a 
broad-based discussion amongst different institutio ns, and we finalise the names 
which we have before us. They are all eminent peopl e. I would like to say that we 
have Dr. Kapila Vatsyayan as the Vice-Chairperson, and Prof. Yashpal, Prof. 
Mrinal Miri, Shri Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Shri Shyam Benegal, Shri Amjad Ali 
Khan, etc. as members of this Committee. All these 14 people, who are members of 
this Committee,- are eminent people. They ared emin ent people in their respective 
fields. The Government can appoint them, and it can  make arrangements for their 
meetings. But, we, simultaneously, keep on requesting them to attend the meetings, 
and contribute as much as they can. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) KAPILA VATSYAYAN: Thank you, Mr. Cha irman, Sir. I 
think that the issue is far more important than set ting up of what is called a central 
advisory board on culture. Mr. Chairman, Sir, throu gh you, I wish to place on 
record here that culture as an administrative unit does not reflect, as Dr. Karan 
Singh has said, the long history of this country in  civilisational terms. It is 
anachronistical today to establish a Department of Culture, which has no connections 
with the Department of Agriculture, to begin with. If the Department of culture is 
disassociated from the fields of rural development,  education, science and the 
creativity of rural India in the craft sector, then  culture becomes a matter only of 
showcasing. Therefore, it is important, and I would like to submit to this House that 
across Party lines we have to think in terms of what constitutes the cultural fabric of 
this country, at the root levels, in terms of the l ife of people. I would also like to 
submit to you, Sir, that the whole fields, which ar e known as the administrative 
fields of culture, institutions, were established l ong ago, and, I happen to be a part 
of that history. But it is time that we look at it again, unless there is an integrated 
view, there can be no question of a cultural policy . The hon. Minister rightly 
mentioned, by quoting my letter, that it was in the  70's, during another regime and 
another international dialogue, that there was a ef fort of, what is called, national 
policies on culture. Even at that time, this Government. ...(Interruption)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put your question. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) KAPILA VATSYAYAN: Sir, I will come to the question in a 
minute. Now even more is no scope, for what is call ed, an administrative official 
cultural policy. My question, therefore, to the hon . Minister is: What steps has the 
Government taken to see that what is called the dom ain of official culture is 
integrated with these other domains, including info rmation and broadcasting? 
Thank you. 
SHRI AJAY MAKEN: Sir, as I said, the Government has  formed the Central 
Advisory Board on Culture of which the hon. Member is the Vice-Chairperson. 
Earlier also, in 2004, the Central Advisory Board o n Culture was formed. Three 
meetings took place of that Central Advisory Board on Culture. Now we have 
made it mandatory that after every three months the  meeting of this Board should 
take place. We hope and expect that this Committee will give some good and 
meaningful suggestions as the hon. Member said, so that we could do the needful. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: Mr. Chairman, Sir , as Kapila 
Vatsyayanji said that there should be an integrated policy as far as culture is concerned 
as regards Education, Ministries of Culture, Inform ation and Broadcasting and 
Science and Technology. Is it not a fact, hon. Mini ster, that after Independence in 
1947, there was a Department of Education,

(a) whether the State Government of Orissa has requested the Centre for grant of

Statement

submitted two memoranda, first memorandum seeking a dditional Central assistance 
of Rs. 306.70 crore from National Calamity Contingency Fund for relief operation in 
the areas affected by heavy rains/ floods in July, 2007 and subsequently second 
memorandum seeking additional Central assistance of Rs. 1093.53 crore for floods of 
August-September, 2007.

Rs. 190 crore for financial assistance for construc tion of saline embankments to

of river mouths of river Mahanadi and Devi under Ma hanadi Basin Development

Commission and comments have been conveyed to the State Government.

SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, my question as to how many districts and lives have been 
affected was not answered. I would like to bring to  the hon. Minister's attention and 
to this House's attention to this news item. This i s from a major national newspaper 
of October 1st. Sir, 25 lakh people have been affec ted, 95 lives have been lost; 3580 
villages have been hit. My point, Sir, is that in the last three years, the floods that have 
repeatedly affected Orissa simply have not got a re sponse from the Central 
Government, and these floods are caused by the lack  of dredging, by the condition 
of the risers and the dams and these are interconnected. 
My point, Sir, is that repeatedly these pleas have been made by the State 
Government and we just do not get enough response. Sir, the Prime Minister himself 
last year was stranded in Bhubaneswar when he visit ed Orissa because for two days 
the thunderstorms and the rains were so strong that  he could not move out of 
Bhubaneswar. He has personally seen the condition o f the State, and, yet, we do not 
get response from the Central Government. 
Sir, my follow-up supplementary question is, in the  last three years we have had 
repeated floods. What were the requests made by the  State Government and how 
much funding has been released in each of the last three years? 
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: As far as the aspect related  to funding is concerned, 
Sir, I have answered the question. It is being examined finally (Interruptions)...  
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, for three years.... (Interruptions)... It is being examined 
for three years! 
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: Mr. Panda's question can be answered within the 
parameters of the question that has been raised. No w you say that we are not 
responding. That is not a fact. You raised the ques tion about saline embankments. 
This is being examined and the Government of India is taking up the matter with the 
World Bank also. You also raised the question of dredging. We are in touch with the 
Orissa Government and all facilities will be provid ed. As far as the disaster and 
sufferings of the people is concerned, I share your  concern, and if I have the 
permission of the House, I can say at this moment t hat I could generate a situation 
of hope here; this is a very vital question. We mus t refuse to wait for the monsoons 
to cause floods in the country. Therefore, it was m y privilege to go to the Cabinet 
with a comprehensive proposal on flood management. It is in the post-monsoon 
period that we could build the embankment and do wh atever we have to do so that 
parts of Bihar, Assam and North Bengal and other ar eas are not submerged. 
Fortunately, Cabinet has agreed with me in principle and we are going to respond to 
the situation. The country must refuse to wait for floods. I had promised the Assam 
Chief Minister, Mr. Gogoi and all the members of th at region that as soon as the 
floods recede, I would visit that area. I went to J orhat, I went to Dibrugarh and I 
went to Majuli. That island is very precious as it has got a 600 year-old Vishnu 
Temple and it is a cultural heritage. So, I went to Majuli and, 1 am not bragging, but 
the

of India (AAI) free of cost and free from all encum brances. AAI is developing and 
upgrading the facilities at these airports which ar e comparable to international 
standards.

Development of pilot training institutes in the country  
*166. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of pilot training institutes (public and private) in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that paucity of such institutes leads to Indian youths having 
to spend a fortune on getting the said training abroad; 
(c) if so, the details of the steps Government is going to take to tackle this problem; 
(d) whether Government is mulling over any plan to intr oduce these institutes at 
various airports of Madhya Pradesh; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI 
PRAFUL PATEL): (a) There are 43 flying training institutes in the country approved by 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) providing training for various licences 
like Private Pilot Licence, Commercial Pilot Licence etc. The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya 
Uran Akademi (IGRUA) is an autonomous society under the Central Government. Of the 
remaining 42 institutes, 27 are run by various State Governments and the balance 15 by 
private enterpreneurs. 
(b) and (c) Training in India or abroad is a matter of individual choice of the trainee. 
The existing flying training institutes in India ar e trying to cope with the increasing 
demand of pilots in the industry. To further ease the situation, the Government has taken 
various steps. These include upgradation and modernisation of training infrastructure of 
Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) to enh ance its training capacity, 
setting up of a world class flying training institute at Gondia, Maharashtra and assistance to 
flying clubs by allocating trainer aircraft through  the Directorate General of Civil 
Aviation/Aero Club of India. 
(d) There is no proposal to develop and flying training institute under the aegis of 
Government of India in Madhya Pradesh. 
(e) Does not arise.

According to the data available, India has a large road network of 3.31 Million Km 
comprising of 66590 Kilometer of National Highways and Expressways, 128000 kilometer 
of State Highways and 3.12 million Kilometer of district and rural roads. The vehicle 
density in India is estimated to be 3.2 motor vehicles per kilometer which is very low. In 
countries like Germany and Taiwan, this figure is m uch higher i.e. 209.6 and 159.2 
respectively. The passener vehicle penetration in India is only 7 cars per thousand people 
whereas in Malaysia, South Korea and Brazil it is 253, 219 and 96 respectively. The 
vehicle penetration in major Indian cities is also very low for example; the vehicle 
penetration for Delhi, Chennai, Mumbai, Kolkata and Bangalore is only 85, 51, 23, 23 and 
41 cars per thousand population respectively. The low vehicle penetration in India is also 
true for two wheelers. Although, India is the second largest producer of two wheelers 
yet the penetration is 43 two wheelers per thousand population as against 258 and 286 in 
Malaysia and Thailand. Therefore, India is hugely under motorized as compared to global 
levels. Inspite of very low vehicle penetration lev els in India as compared to global 
levels, the congestion problem in Metro-cities arises due to factors like driving conditions, 
driver behaviour, enforcement of rules and regulations, traffic management, lack of town 
planning etc. However, there is continued effort for improvement of road infrastructure in 
the country. 
Currently, the automotive sector in India accounts for 5% of GDP. The sector 
provides direct and indirect employment to 13.1 mil lion people and also facilitates 
economic growth. Therefore, Government is not considering freezing production of more 
cars. Instead, there is continuous effort to improve driving conditions and mass transit 
systems for decongestions. 
Oil reserves in the country  
*168.    SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the BP Statistical Review of World Energy 2007 released by the British 
Multinational has pointed out that India's oil reserves would last just another 19.3 years at 
the current rate of production and the last year study had revealed India's reserves would 
last about 20 years; 

Written Answers to [27- NOV. 2007]         Starred Questions     23 
(b) whether the lower estimate now reflects the country 's inability to add to its 
proven oil reserves; 
(c) if so, what are the concrete steps and measures Gov ernment proposes to take 
to improve the position in future; and 
(d) whether any concrete measure is being considered in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MUR LI 
DEORA): (a) to (d) BP statistical review of world e nergy 2007 has pointed out that 
reserve to production (R/P) ratio for India is 19.3 years at current rate of production 
and assuming that no reserves are added in next 19 to 20 years. In last five years, 
reserve replacement ratio (RRR) in India was more t han one, which means, oil 
companies in India have accreted more reserves than their oil and gas production. The 
balance recoverable reserve position in 2002-03 was  about 1485.73 million metric 
tonnes of oil and oil equivalent of gas (MMTOE), wh ich has increased to 1843.15 
MMTOE in 2006-07 achieving an increase of 24%. 
In order to enhance hydrocarbon security for the co untry, the significant steps 
initiated by the Government and public sector undertakings for meeting the demand of 
petroleum products in the country, inter alia include: 
(i) incerasing exploration efforts through the New Exploration Licensing 
Policy (NELP) and exploring new areas, especially i n deep waters and 
difficult frontier areas, as also the deeper layers  of already producing 
fields; 
(ii) improving the recovery factor from existing ma jor fields by 
implementing Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR)/Improved O il Recovery 
(IOR) schemes; 
(iii) developing newly discovered fields speedily a nd stepping up the use of 
new technologies for seismic surveys, work over, st imulation operations, 
drilling of wells, etc., in producing areas; 
(iv) acquisition of oil and gas assets abroad in or der to ensure hydrocarbon 
security for the country; 
(v)   Exploring potential of alternate sources; 
(vi)  Conservation of petroleum products.

Standby X-ray machines at metro airports 
 *170.  SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the logic in having standby X-ray machines at metro airports in the country 
despite shortage of space; and 
(b) if it is not rationale, whether Government would stop such practice, which is national 
waste? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL 
PATEL): (a) X-ray machines are used for non-invasive screening of passengers' baggages by 
security staff at the airports. These X-ray machines, like other elector-mechanical equipment, 
are prone to unserviceable contingencies. 
During such contingencies, preventive and/or breakdown maintenance, the relevant X-ray 
machine is not available for use. Repair of X-ray machine sometimes takes long hours. During 
this period, operation of flight at the airport gets affected. In order to overcome the problem, 
standby X-ray machines have been provided at major airports. 
All the security related equipment have been installed as per the requirements and 
technical specifications prescribed by the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS). 
(b) Does not arise. 
Exposure of public sector banks to realty and capital market sectors 
* 171. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the public sector banks, because of their increased exposure to realty and 
capital market sectors, would suffer in the event of repetition of boom-burst cycles; 
(b) if so, whether any measures have been initiated to contionuously monitor the situation 
and plug the systemic problems that may crop up and advise the banks to reduce their 
exposure to the said sector; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) The exposure 
of public sector banks (PSBs) to real estate and capital market sectors has increased during the 
period March, 2006 to March, 2007. However, the growth of such exposure, as a percentage 
of gross advances, is marginal. 

Written Answers to [27 NOV. 2007]         Starred Questions     25 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) monitors the exposure of banks to realty and capital 
market sectors on a continual basis, and issues, guidelines to the banks, as and when 
required. RBI has taken various measures to minimiz e the risks arising out of 
financing to real estate and capital market sectors which inter alia, include enhancing 
risk weights and provisioning requirements for bank 's exposure to these sectors; 
advising the banks to put in place a contorl mechan ism for managing risks involved 
in the housing sector; advising the banks to intiat e preventive and corrective 
measures regarding real estate sector and explicitl y prescribe internal ceilings for 
such exposures; prescribing minimum internal rating required for builders; prescribing 
requisite security cover to be kept; and rationalis ation of prudential capital market 
exposure norms. RBI has also issued guidelines to t he banks with regard to their 
advances against share. Further, all public sector banks have put in place a robust risk 
management system to effectively manage risks arisi ng out of their credit and 
investment portfolios.

Constant increase in monetary liquidity  
†*176. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Mini ster of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the pressure of monetary liquidity is increasing 
constantly due to increasing flow of funds in the e conomy and it is not stopping 
despite increasing Cash Reserve Ratio twice; 
(b) what are the suggestions given by the Rangarajan Co mmittee in this dregard 
and the alternatives proposed; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answers to [27-NOV. 2007]         Starred Questions     29 
(c) whether the dollar bonds bought by the Reserve Bank  of India would be 
affected by declining value of dollar; and 
(d) whether the process of their purchasing and selling would affect the 
liquidity? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) The injection 
liquidity in the domestic economy due to the foreign exchange market operations of the 
RBI is modulated by monetary policy instruments available to the RBI. RBI change 
the prescribed Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) from time t o time based on the emerging 
liquidity situation. As CRR is not the only monetar y instrument to absord excess 
liquidity, it will not be appropriate to judge the regulation of liquidity solely by the 
changes in CRR. RBI has successively increased the CRR on four occasions from a 
level of 6 per cent as on March 3, 2007 to reach a level of 7.50 per cent as on 
November, 10,2007. 
(b) The "Economic Outlook for 2007-08" brought out by t he Economic Advisory 
Council to the Prime Minister in July, 2007 identif ies the following options in the 
context of strong capital flows, viz., (i) let the rupee appreciate, (ii) absorb the 
capital flows into capital reserves and sterilize t he excess over what may be 
regarded as appropriate, and (iii) liberalies outfl ows by removing admministrative 
and procedural implements and to discourage inflows  by putting restrictions on 
some capital items. Since there are limits to which  each instrument can be used by 
itself, the Economic Advisory Council recommended ajudicious mix of all the three 
instruments. 
(c) Foreign exchange reserves held by the Reserve Bank of India are 
denominated in US dollars and as such the value of the bond denominated in 
dollars would not be affected by declining value of  the dollar. However, the value 
when translated to Indian Rupees for accounting purposes, would be affected by the 
appreciation or depreciation of the US dollar against the Indian Rupee. 
(d) The process of buying and selling of bonds denomina ted in US dollars by the 
Reserve Bank of India, as part of reserve management, is done in the overseas market 
and as such, does not affect the domestic liquidity situation.

macro-economic environment, growth potential of the economy, corporate performance, 
domestic and international events, and market sentiments. The fluctuations in October,

derivative instruments, sub-prime crisis in the USA, interest rate cut by the US Fed,

Review of interest rate  
756. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether any steps are being taken to encourage Minority-focused Banks by the 
(a) whether Government has reviewed the interest rate scenario; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what is the demand indicated by the economy; 
(d) whether any correctives are warranted by the economic conditions; and 
(e) if so the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Effective from October 18,1994, the Reserve 
Bank of India (RBI) has deregulated the interest rates on advances above Rs. 2 lakhs, 
including the housing loans and these interest rate s are determined by the banks 
themselves with the approval of their Boards of Directors subject to Banchmark Prime 
Lending Rates (BPLR) and spread guidelines. In order to enhance transparency in banks' 
pricing of their loan products, banks have been advised to fix their BPLR after taking into 
account (i) actual cost of funds (ii) operating expenses and (iii) a minimum margin to cover 
regulatory requirement of provisioning/ capital charge and profit margin and ensure that 
the BPLR truly reflects the actual cost. Individual banks, therefore, determine interest 
rates to be charged to a particular borrower subjec t to BPLR and spread guidelines. 
Given the prevailing credit market in India and the need to continue with concessionality 
for small borrowers, the practice of treating BPLR as the ceiling for loans upto Rs. two 
lakhs continues. However, Banks are free to determi ne the rates of interest without 
reference to BPLR and regardless of the size in res pect of loans of purchase of 
consumer durables, loans to individuals against sha res and debentures/bonds, other 
non-priority sector personal loans, etc. 
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has given freedom to commercial banks with effect 
from 22nd October, 1997 to fix. their own interest rates on domestic term deposits of 
various maturities with the prior approval of their respective Board of Directors/Asset 
Liability Management Committee (ALCO). As such, the rates of interest on deposits are 
determined by the banks themselves. 
(c) to (e) RBI had stated that the outcome for interest rates depends mainly on the 
outlook for inflation, growth prospects and investment demand and it is not possible to 
predict short-run movements in interest rates.

AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) and (b) As passing on the entire 
impact of the steep increase in the oil prices to t he consumers would have resulted 
in hardship to the common man, as the retail sellin g prices of petrol, diesel, PDS 
Kerosene and domestic LPG have not been correspondi ng to the increase in the 
prices of crude oil and  petroleum products in the international market.

cylinders at their godown before delivery at the cu stomers premises. In a bid to 
enhance customer satisfaction levels, distributors in selected markets have been 
advised by OMCs to provide a spring balance to enab le the customers to verify the 
correctness of the weight of LPG in the  cylinder. OMCs have introduced this 
scheme in major markets of the country. 
The officials of OMCs carry out random checks at di stributors godowns, 
delivery points, as well as en-route to ensure that  no pilferage takes place. The 
distributors of OMCs are under strict instructions to check the weight of cylinders at 
their godowns before delivery, and only cylinders with the specified weighted are to 
be delivered to the customers. The distributors hav e also been instructed to ensure 
that the seals are verified and shown to the custom ers at the time of delivery. In 
case any underweight cylinder is received by the cu stomer, such cylinders are 
repeated with a fresh refill cylinder without any charges levised by the OMCs.

pricing so that the Energy Co-ordination Committee will take final decision on 
fixing of the gas price;

gas pricing policy which are equitable and conduciv e to the development of this 
sector; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a), (c) and (d ) Government 
constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGoM) to consider issues relating 
to pricing and commercial utilization of natural ga s under NELP. EGoM has 
decided the issue of pricing of gas under NELP. The  EGoM has also decided that 
the price discovery process on arms length basis wi ll be adopted in the fututre 
NELP contracts only after the approval of the price  basis/formula by the 
Government. They have also decided that the price d iscovered through this process 
would be applicable to all the sectors, uniformly. 
(b) The price of gas produced by ONGC and OIL from the blocks allotted to 
them on nomination basis is determined by the Gover nment; this constitutes 
Administrative Pricing Mechanism (APM) gas. The gas  produced by Joint 
Ventures (JVs)/Private Companies is available at price determined by the respective 
Production Sharing Contract (PSC). As regards LNG, while the price of LNG 
imported under term contracts is governed by the SP A between the LNG seller and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY. OF WATER RES OURCES

Policy, 2002 (NWP) has laid due emphasis on water m anagement. The NWP states 
that there should be an integrated and multi-discip linary approach to planning, 
development, conservation and management of water r esources. The Policy also 
states that adequate emphasis need to be given to p hysical and financial

The Government of India have formulated a National Perspective Plan for Water 
Resources Development (NPP) in August, 1980. The NP P comprises of two 
components viz. (i) Peninsular Rivers Development and (ii) Himalaya n Rivers 
Development and envisages construction of storages on various river systems along 
with interlinking canal systems to transfer water f rom water surplus areas to water 
deficit regions. National Water DevelopmentAgency ( NWDA) under Ministry of 
Water Resources has been set up in 1982 to study th e feasibility of inter basin water 
transfer proposals and give a concrete shape to NPP . NWDA after various studies 
identified 30 links under NPP. Out of the 30 links,  five links have been prioritized 
for their implementation. The prioritized links are  (i) Ken-Betwa link (ii) Parbati-
Kalisindh-Chambal link (iii) Dmanaganga-Pinjal link  (iv) Par-Tapi-Narmada link, 
and (v) Godavari (Polavaram)-Krishna (Vijayawada) link.

KUMAR DEEPAK DAS (Assam): There is no judicial inqu iry. There is only

SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Thank you for the correction . So, we want the 
Assam Government to take immediate action. The othe r very important point to 
which I would like to draw the attention of the House is the fate of the Forest Rights 
Bill which was unanimously passed by Parliament one year ago. It is shocking and it 
is completely violative of Parliamentary procedures that for one year the rules have 
not been notified as a result of which all over the  country in many States a large 
number of adivasis are being evicted from their homes and lands in the forests. And 
what is even more shocking is that the rules have n ot been notified and that is why 
the Act is not being implemented. 
One section of the Act which pertains to the identi fication of critical wildlife 
habitat, which once identified may lead to modification of the rights of adivasis in a 
forest leading to their relocation and eviction, is  being implemented without the 
notification of the rules. How can this be done? 
The sequencing of the Act is, first recognise and v est the forest rights in all 
adivasis, including in protected areas. The second part of th e Act is, through a 
case-by-case basis inprotected areas and through th e formation of an Expert 
Committee on the basis of scientific evidence, crit ical wildlife habitat may be 
identified and where necessary adivasis may be relocated according to certain 
procedures. 
So, first of all, the rules not being notified is a  subversion of the will of 
Parliament, because it means that the Act unanimous ly passed is not being 
implemented. Secondly, one portion of the Act is be ing implemented without the 
rules being notified is a second subversion of Parliament and also a subversion of the 
spirit and letter of the Act itself. And the third important point is, instead of 
recognising the rights of  adivasis in all forest areas, as mandated by the Act, the 
Government of India is changing the sequencing of the Act by these actions. 
Therefore, I believe that this is a very, very seri ous matter. Large numebrs of 
adivasis are being evicted from forests. I hope the House will join me in urging the 
Government not to subvert the will of Parliament, a nd to immediately enact the 
rules, notify the Rules, and implemented the Act.

NEED FOR PROTECTING INDIAN FISHERMEN FROM HARASSMENT BY  
SRI LANKAN NAVY  
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY (Puducherry): Mr. Deputy Chair man, thank you 
for giving me this opportunity. After a long time, 1 am making a Zero Hour 
submission. This is a matter of concern for all of us. The Indian fishermen, living in 
the coastal areas of Tamil Nadu, when they go for fishing in Indian maritime waters 
near the Sri Lankan border, the Sri Lankan Navy, un der the-guise that the Indian 
fishermen crossed over to their territory, takes th em into custody, takes them to Sri 
Lanka, keeps them in their jail and after due inter vention by the Government of 
India and also by the hon.Chief Minister of Tamil N adu release them. It happened 
on several occasions. 
Sir, you know pretty well that the Government of In dia gave Kachchativu to Sri 
Lanka for the purpose of drying nets. What happens is that when our Indian 
fishermen go for fishing, when there is inclement w eather, they go to Kachchativu 
for drying the fish and their nets. They have been taken into custody from there 
also. They have got a lot of sophisticated weapons.  Sometimes, they take away 
their boats and damage the boats of Indian fisherme n also. The fishermen from 
Nagapattinam, Tuticorin, Rameswaram, Nagercoil, etc ., are affected and their 
families have been suffering. This issue has been t aken up by the Tamil Nadu 
Government with the hon. Prime Minister and the hon . External Affairs Minister 
also. This is a matter of very serious concern. Lakhs of fishermen families are insecure 
in those area. On the one side, the Sri Lankan Navy is taking them into custody and, 
on the other ,the LITE, the terrorist group, is att acking them in the mid-sea. That is 
how our fishermen are affected. Therefore, this is a matter of serious concern for al 
of us and, day in, day out, news items are appearin g. Twelve fishermen from 
Nagapattinam have been taken into custody by the Sr i Lankan Navy and the LTTE 
threatened them, took their boats and removed the d iesel from the boats and put 
them in the mid-sea. This is the harassment caused to our fishermen it is the duty of 
the Government of India to protect the Indian fishermen from being harassed by the 
Sri Lankan Navy Force and the terrorist groups. The refore, to put an end to this, I 
want the hon. Minister of External Affairs to take up the issue with the Sri Lankan 
Government, talk to them and to give protection to Indian fishermen. Let the Sri 
Lankan Navy not harass Indian fishermen who go for fishing for their livelihood. 
Otherwise, there will be tension in those areas. If  the people in the coastal areas 
revolt, there will be tension; and there will be la w and order problem in the coastal 
areas of Tamil Nadu. Therefore, I wanted to raise this issue. Now the hon. Minister of 
State for External Affairs is here. You can ask him . If he wants to respond, he can 
respond.

SHRI D. RAJA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, it is good that the  hon. HRD Minister is

Rural Health Mission. I do understand the concern o f the Government, the concern 
of al political parties to improve the health servi ces in villages and rural areas. 
Having said this, I must point out that there is a lot of confusion as far as 
recruitment policy is concerned. And the UPA Government must come clear on this 
recruitment policy Now, it is said that in the name  of compulsory rural services, the 
duration of MBBS course is lengthened. As of now, t he duration of the MBBS 
course is four-and-a-half years plus one- year inte rnship. Now, this duration has 
been increased from five-and-a-half years to six-and-a-half years. This has led to a lot 
of apprehension and agitation not only in Tamil Nad u but also several other States.

services. It is of nobody's argument that rural hea lth services must be made

for rural services, actually four months are to be served in District Headquarters 
hospitals; four months in Tehsil hospitals and only  four months in villages. They 
are just students, and

SPECIAL MENTIONS  
Concern over proliferation of explosives and small  arms 
SHRI SANTOSH-BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): I rise to commend the attention of this 
House to the recent reports suggesting proliferation of explosives and small arms among 
unauthorised and potentially subversive elements. During 2004-06, 86000 detonators, 
20MT slurry explosive, 52 kms. of detonating fuse a nd about half MT of explosive 
Gelatine sticks have been stolen or diverted to such elements from some 21000 licensed 
explosive manufacturers. Explosive substances like ammonium nitrate and potassium 
chlorate that were used in recent blasts are available freely in the market. The geographical 
spread of such thefts is confined largely to naxal-infested areas of Chhattisgarh, Orissa, 
Jharkhand and Marathwada. Another associated challenge for internal security is the 
spread of assult arms among subversive groups, organised crime-gangs and country-made 
arms in the rural areas. The recent seizures suggest that such arms are either of the foreign 
origin or have been stolen from Ordnance factories or illegally assembled by unauthorised 
manufacturers. Even more alarming is the pilferage from the Ordnance factories and 
Government arms depots.

Collectively, such trends present a scary scenario for the internal security situation. I 
ask the Government to enhance the surveillance to trace the leads of such pilferages and 
present them. Beyond customary advisory to State Home Departments, the Government 
must issue stringent guidelines to district police to stem the proliferation of explosive 
substances and small assault arms. Internal security nonetheless is a Central-subject. 
Concern over Para-military and Armed Forces personnel quitting jobs  
under stress  
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): Sir, it is a matter of grave concern 
that India's first line of defence, BSF, is putting away their weapons and going home 
for good. Nearly 41,000 Border Security Force personnel—one in five in the 2.09 lakh 
force—have quit their jobs over the last 30 months.  Over 7,000 men deployed along 
the Indo-Pakistan and Indo-Bangladesh borders put in their papers in the first half of 
2007; nearly 16,200 quit in 2006 and more than 17,000 in 200S. Most of them were from 
the constabulary and had spent the prime of their lives at the border. An annual attrition 
rate of 8 per cent was alarming. 
But, BSF personnel are not the only one giving up their jobs. Over 2,000 people quit 
the CRPF, a 2.48 lakh strong force; nearly half as many resign from the Central Industrial 
Security Force annually and 1,500 from the Assam Rifles, the force deployed to fight 
insurgents in the North-East. 
Unfortunately, BSF has a suicide rate that is three times higher than the army. Last year, 
41 BSF personnel committed suicide against 100 Army personnel; the BSF's suicide 
rate was 20.5 per lakh against 6.6 per lakh in the Army. Obviously, our security forces 
have had enough of the tough life, long periods away from home and few rewards. 
In view of the above alarming scenario, I would urge the hon. Home Minister to take 
corrective measures on war-footing. 
[The Vice-Chairman (SHRI UDYA PARTAP SINGH) in the chair] 
Need to identify Bhoodan lands for distribution among poor 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA (Maharashtra): Sir, Ekta Parishad's five year long progressive 
and intensified campaign-now metamorphosis as Janad esh 2007—is a non-violent 
movement to project people's land rights and obtain  Government's commitment for 
immediate interaction, about 25000 dedicated landless farmers and have-nots from 18 
States, having spontaneous support of about 1000 foreign nationals from 19 countries 
also walked all the way (360 kms) to show their solidarity for the cause. This reminds me 
of the Bhoodan Yajona-the Lands Gift Mission—in fif ties' under the leadership of 
Mahatma Gandhi's foremost disciple, Acharya Vinobha have, along with well-known 
social activists like Ms. Nirmala Deshpande and Shr i Lalu Dada originating from 
Pochampalli, Andhra Pradesh and selfless Sarvodaya workers, walked from village to 
village for 13 years covering 50,000 Kms, persuading people to share the land with their 
landless brethern. Over ten lakh hectares of land was collected as Bhoodan, of which 40 
per cent could be distributed to the landless. The remaining 60 per cent could not be 
distributed in the absence of a supportive legislat ion and political will. The nation's 
consciousness has to return once again to the tradi tional land rights of Advasis and 
landless who are denied either in the name of development or thorough manipulations of the 
land mafia. Government's immediate initiative in the shape of setting up an expert 
committee followed by the National Land Reforms Council is a laudable augury. For 
giving immediate relief, the Goverment should initiate identification of Bhoodan lands 
in various States that are yet to be distributed. T he Government should provide 
legislative and other necessary support to responsi ble NGOs and complete the 
unfinished task of Acharya Vinobha Bhaveji. This wi ll be our contribution in the 
centenary year of Satyagraha Movemnet and fulfilment of Mahatma Gandhi's prayer to 
wipe tear from every eye of the poorest of the poor. Thank you.

Need to take effective measures for abolishing Child Labour 
SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-C hairman, Sir, I 
would like to draw the attention of Central Governm ent towards abolishing of child 
labour problem in our country. Sir, according to th e India Census of 1991, there are 
11.28 million working children under the age of fou rteen years in India. Over 85 
percent of this child labour is in the country's ru ral areas, working in agricultural 
activities such as farming, hotels, dhabas, livesto ck rearing, forestry and fisheries 
etc. Sir, as a developing country, our country is f acing a multitude of social 
problems. India has adopted constitutional statutor y and developmental measures 
with a view to eliminate it. Child labour is caused  by a multitdue of problems 
including poverty, unemployment/underemployment, il literacy, lack of school 
facilities and inefficiency of protective legislati on for working children. In order to 
overcome these problems, our country must first rec ognize that child labour exists 
in the different parts of the country and it should  be eradicated. Sir, as the 
Government is aware that forced, bonded or indentur ed child labour is prohibited 
under Indian laws but it is a matter of grave conce rn to all of us that existing laws, 
including Child Labour (prohibition and regulation)  Act, 1986 are not being 
implemented effectively throughout the country by t he Government. The Central 
Government should give suitable directions to the c oncerned State Governments to 
implement it in an effective manner. Therefore, I u rge upon the Central 
Government to formulate and chalk out a legal action plan and the specific programs 
and schemes to abolish child labour from the country. Thank you.
